analysis.one_liner: Ends royalty discounts for oil and gas drilling on federal land and caps the costs companies deduct from royalties.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since its introduction, with no vote, no hearing scheduled, and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that drill for oil and gas on federal land and offshore waters pay the government a share of what they produce. Under current law, those companies can get discounts on their royalties and can subtract their transportation costs — sometimes generously estimated — before paying. This bill would repeal the discount programs, cap the transportation deduction at the lesser of 30 percent of the production's value or its actual reasonable cost, and require federal agencies to report each year on how many royalty discounts were granted and what they cost the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state treasuries, and ultimately taxpayers, who would collect a larger share of the value of oil and gas taken from publicly owned land and waters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, through higher federal royalty collections

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 344 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005, the law that lets companies drilling in the Gulf of Mexico pay reduced royalties on some deep-water wells [S2].
Eliminates royalty discounts for offshore Alaska planning areas and for production from the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, requiring full royalty payments [S2].

Caps the transportation allowance companies may deduct from their royalty payments at the lesser of 30 percent of production value or actual reasonable costs, and requires standardized rates by region — closing a channel where inflated cost estimates have reduced what companies pay [S2].

Requires annual reports from the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Ocean Energy Management detailing how many royalty relief applications were approved, how many wells got relief, and the estimated revenue difference — making the discounts visible to Congress and the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies producing on federal land and offshore leases, which would pay higher effective royalties and smaller cost deductions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

drawbacks.text: Higher effective royalties and a capped transportation deduction would raise costs for companies drilling on federal leases, which the industry argues could reduce drilling on federal land and push some production to state and private lands [S2].

A flat 30 percent cap may not reflect the real spread of transportation costs across regions, so companies facing genuinely high transport expenses would still pay royalties as if those costs were lower [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core effect is straightforward: companies would pay closer to full royalties on oil and gas taken from publicly owned resources, and the discounts would become visible in annual reports. The trade-off is that higher costs could discourage some federal-lease drilling, with possible effects on domestic production. The scale of that trade-off is contested and the bill itself contains no projections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2026 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the bill on September 3, 2026, with 19 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and no further action appears in the record [S4].
No Republican has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled in committee, oil and gas companies continue receiving royalty discounts and generous transportation deductions on federal leases, and the Treasury continues collecting the lower amounts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies keep their royalty discounts

for.name: Maxine Dexter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup since its referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority controls the committee calendar [S3].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands and waters
industries.note: The bill would end royalty discounts in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska and cap the transportation deductions companies subtract from royalty payments, raising what they owe on federal leases. The industry's interest in keeping the discounts runs against taxpayers' interest in collecting full value for public resources.

analysis.trajectory: With only minority-party support, no Republican cosponsor, and a referral to a committee chaired by the opposing party, the bill's most likely path is to die quietly at the end of the session without a hearing or vote.
